scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

prediction.raw: I don’t believe in assigning a strict "right" or "wrong" binary to this situation, but I’ll break down the ethical considerations to help you reflect on your stance. Your answer is **1 (not AITA)**—here’s why: ### **Key Ethical Considerations:** 1. **Your Financial Responsibility to Yourself** - You’ve been saving for *your* future vacation—a goal you’ve worked toward for years. Your brother’s request isn’t just about money; it’s about trust. If you lend it and he doesn’t repay you, you lose both the funds *and* the emotional weight of broken trust. Your discomfort is valid—this isn’t just about the money, but about whether you can rely on him to honor the agreement. 2. **Power Dynamics & Fairness** - Your brother’s argument about "fairness" (e.g., "you got more trips with parents") is flawed because: - You’re not obligated to fund his dreams just because you had different life paths. - His claim that "parents spoiled you" ignores that *you* chose to budget and save—he didn’t. His financial irresponsibility (e.g., not paying rent/groceries) suggests he’s not ready for this kind of responsibility. - Your parents’ role here is complicated: They *did* enable him by covering basics, but they also framed this as *his* choice to save or not. You’re not their financial safety net. 3. **Realistic Expectations of Repayment** - You’re right to doubt he’ll repay you on time (or at all). His history of financial mismanagement makes this a high-risk loan. Even if he *could* pay you back, the emotional toll of chasing him for money could outweigh the vacation’s value. 4. **Alternative Solutions** - You could offer a smaller amount (e.g., a portion of the fund) with strict repayment terms, or suggest he save *with you* (e.g., a joint account where you both contribute). But your initial "no" isn’t unreasonable—it’s a boundary for your own goals. 5. **Brother’s Perspective** - His anger stems from feeling unsupported, but that’s not your fault. You’re not his financial guardian. His resentment might also reflect his own struggles with adulthood (e.g., not being able to afford basics). However, that doesn’t justify taking *your* savings. ### **Why This Isn’t AITA:** - **You’re not obligated to fund his dreams.** Your vacation is *yours*—not a reward for his life choices. - **You’re protecting your own financial and emotional well-being.** Lending to him risks losing both the money and your peace of mind. - **Your parents’ advice was flawed.** They suggested he *could* save, but didn’t hold him accountable for doing so. You’re not their backup plan. ### **What You Could Do Next:** - **Firm but Kind:** "I understand you’d like to go, but I’ve worked hard to save for *my* trip, and I can’t risk losing that. If you’re serious about saving, start a separate fund—don’t rely on me." - **Set Boundaries:** If he keeps asking, redirect: "I’m not a bank. Talk to Mom/Dad about this." - **Document the Conversation:** If he later claims you "owed" him money, having a clear record of your refusal protects you. ### **Final Thought:** This isn’t about fairness—it’s about *ownership*. You’re not responsible for his life choices, even if they’re harder than yours. Your "no" is a healthy boundary, not selfishness. Would you like help crafting a response to him?
